lines.text: Prediction markets have a problem AI looks perfect for.
And a reason you should never hand AI the keys.
AuspeX is built on that tension. A prediction market platform on MST Blockchain Testnet, resting on one sentence.
AI proposes. Humans and the chain decide.
Two things break prediction markets.
Writing a good one is hard. Will the economy improve is unresolvable, and disputes are guaranteed.
And research does not scale, so most people bet on vibes.
AI is good at both jobs. So the question is not whether AI can do this, but how you let it, without giving it authority.
AuspeX puts AI everywhere it is useful, and nowhere it is authoritative.
A model may only propose. Which headlines describe one event. A draft question. A stake as a fraction of a cap it never sees.
Deterministic code decides. Pure functions, no network, no model.
This role matrix is live. Every cell is an eth_call made when the page loaded. It asks the contract rather than telling you.
It starts with real news feeds.
Clustering is deterministic first. Score above one half on weighted headline similarity and two articles merge with no model involved. Below one quarter, never.
Only the ambiguous band between is shown to an LLM.
And a story needs two distinct publishers before it can become a market.
If the model is rate limited, the answer is do not merge. A failing dependency takes no action and stays up.
The AI drafts a specification. A human sees a checklist, not a paragraph.
Ambiguity is easier to catch in a checklist, and catching it here matters, because no money exists yet.
The source headlines are fenced off as untrusted. They reached the model in delimited tags, in a user message, never a system instruction.
Then a person signs createMarket in a browser wallet. Only now does anything reach the chain.
Sent by the human authority wallet, not the deployer. That key lives only in a browser extension. This repository has never seen it.
Members bet through agents. Each proposes a side, a confidence and a stake, and decides none of them.
A deterministic gate clamps it against six limits, recording every refusal. Then the contract caps it again.
Off chain in blue, on chain in purple. Bounded twice. By code that does not trust the model, and by a chain that does not trust us.
And payouts go to the member's owner address, never the agent. A stolen agent key can lose its capped stake. It cannot steal winnings.
Everything so far is my code. My code can be wrong, or compromised.
So here is the layer that does not depend on me at all.
This button is on the public site. It needs no wallet. Anyone watching this can press it.
It asks an agent to bet exactly one wei more than its on-chain cap.
Reverted.
The attempt was one wei above a cap of zero point zero two tMSTC, and the contract put both numbers in the error.
So with my server fully compromised and every off-chain check bypassed, that agent cannot exceed its cap. The chain refuses it.
A failed transaction is not a bug here. It is the product.
Three things I want to be straight about.
Resolution is trusted. An authorised set, an evidence URL on chain, a challenge window, permissionless finalisation. That bounds a bad resolver. It is not a decentralised oracle.
The market creator and the resolver are currently the same wallet, and they should not be.
And the organisers' Fortuna VRF contract has no bytecode on this testnet. So randomised resolver selection was cut, rather than faked.
Do not take my word for any of it.
Every hash here is re-fetched from the explorer by a script that fails if one disagrees.
It is live right now. Go and press the button yourself.
